newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks harmony on "partial birth" abortions.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks harmony on "partial birth" abortions.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Friday any law on the contentious issue of so-called partial birth abortion should make sure the procedure remained available to the few women who truly need it.

"I would like to see us bring some harmony to this and put it behind us," Clinton said at a televised news conference. He vetoed a bill to ban the procedure last year surrounded by five women who had undergone the abortions, most of whom had harrowing stories of late-term pregnancies gone awry.

"I think you could make a very compelling case that for the small number of people I'm trying to protect this is the biggest issue in their entire lives and that for them my position is the pro-life position," Clinton said.

"And I believe that it would be a mistake for us to pass this bill one more time without taking care of those folks," he added two days after a new bill banning the procedure was introduced in the House of Representatives.

Clinton has said he would be able to sign a bill that allowed the procedure to be performed to save the life or health of the woman. The current bill, like last year's, provides only for cases where the woman's life is at stake.

The issue has sparked heated debate since a ban was first introduced in Congress in 1995. The procedure involves the partial extraction of the foetus feet-first, the subsequent suctioning out of the foetal brain and removal of the foetus.

The latest flareup began last week when Ron Fitzsimmons, executive director of the National Coalition of Abortion Providers, said he "lied through my teeth" when he defended this kind of late-term abortion.
Instead of the 500 or so a year cited by abortion rights advocates, he said as many as 5,000 might be performed, many on women in earlier stages of non-crisis pregnancies.

Clinton, whose position on abortion has been that it should be safe, legal and rare, turned aside a question about the actual number of these procedures, saying his primary concern was the few women for whom there was no alternative.

Referring to the women who visited the White House for his veto, he said, "They were told that unless they had a procedure which would be banned under the law that I vetoed, after it was over the babies they were carrying would be dead and their bodies would never be able to have another baby. That is my only concern."

Asked if he would consider signing the current bill, he said he wanted to see the language to make sure women in earlier stages of pregnancy who want elective abortions will have alternatives to the so-called partial birth method.

He said the proposed ban "might not work to reduce the overall number of abortions at all, but in the end what it could do is every year to take a few hundred women and wreck their lives and wreck the possibility that they could have further children."
